# Obesity & metabolic syndrome

> *Obesity and the metabolic syndrome result from biology and environment together, and a normal BMI can
> still coexist with harmful visceral fat. We cover how weight status and the metabolic syndrome are defined, how
> excess fat produces the cluster of risks, lifestyle-first dietary management delivered without stigma,
> and when to refer.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Classify an adult's weight status on Singapore's lower BMI and waist cut-offs, and explain why
  Singapore acts earlier than the WHO cut-offs.
- Apply the harmonised any-three-of-five definition of the metabolic syndrome, and explain why it is a
  risk marker and not a single disease.
- Explain how visceral and ectopic fat, adipose inflammation and the adipokine shift produce insulin
  resistance and the metabolic-syndrome cluster.
- Explain why ultra-processed foods and sugar-sweetened drinks drive overeating: what is eaten shapes
  how much is eaten.
- Plan lifestyle-first care across diet, activity, sleep, stress and behaviour change aimed at a
  5–10% loss, and recognise medication and surgery as specialist tiers to refer for.
- Frame a weight conversation in weight-inclusive, person-first language, and explain why weight
  stigma harms health.
:::

## Obesity & metabolic syndrome at a glance {#sec-overview}

Over- and under-nutrition are the two forms of malnutrition, and obesity is the more familiar one
(undernutrition is in the *Undernutrition & malnutrition* chapter). Obesity also commonly precedes
other cardiometabolic disease, because the same central, insulin-resistant fat that defines it drives much
of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease (see the *Type 2 diabetes* and *Cardiovascular disease &
hypertension* chapters).

Three ideas shape how over-nutrition is recognised and managed:

- Singapore acts at lower BMI and waist cut-offs than the global ones, for a physiological reason.
- Diet quality matters more than calorie counting alone, and sleep and stress are modifiable factors
  too.
- How a weight conversation is framed, without stigma and with the person first, is part of clinical
  care.

The underlying physiology (how energy balance is measured, and how leptin, ghrelin and the
hypothalamus set appetite) is in the [*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd) and
[*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd) chapters.

## Pathophysiology: why the risks cluster and the weight accumulates {#sec-science}

### Defining obesity and the metabolic syndrome {#sec-recognising}

#### Classifying weight status: BMI, waist and why Singapore acts earlier {#sec-phenotype}

BMI (weight ÷ height², introduced in the [*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd#sec-measuring)
chapter) is a screening proxy, not a measurement of fat. It does not distinguish muscle from fat or show
where the fat sits. That limitation matters in Singapore, because Singaporean adults carry more body
fat, and proportionally more visceral fat, at a given BMI than the Western populations on which the
WHO cut-offs were built.

The local Yishun Study demonstrated this difference. Matched for BMI, age and sex, Singaporeans had higher
percentage body fat than white adults in the US and Europe, and classifying by body fat
identified far more adults with excess body fat than BMI did [@chen2021yishun]. Because Asians reach diabetes and cardiovascular risk
at a lower BMI, Singapore sets its action points below the WHO cut-offs
[@whoExpert2004AsianBMI].

There are therefore two sets of BMI cut-offs:

| Cut-off set | Lower threshold | Upper threshold |
|---|---|---|
| WHO (global) | Overweight: BMI ≥25 kg/m² | Obese: BMI ≥30 kg/m² |
| Singapore (clinical action) [@hpbmoh2016obesityCPG; @sgObesityBMI] | Intervene: BMI ≥23 kg/m² | High risk: BMI ≥27.5 kg/m² |

The most useful additional bedside measure is waist circumference, because it reflects central fat, the
metabolically active kind. The Asian cut-offs are lower here too: ≥90 cm in men and ≥80 cm in women
[@alberti2009harmonizingMetS; @sgObesityBMI]. A waist at or above the cut-off defines **central
obesity**, excess fat carried around the abdomen. BMI and waist circumference are therefore interpreted together, never
BMI alone.

::: {.example}
A patient with a "reassuring" BMI of 24 kg/m² and a waist over the cut-off is still at increased risk.
:::

#### The metabolic syndrome: a cluster, not a disease {#sec-mets}

Central fat is rarely the only abnormality. The **metabolic syndrome** is the tendency for five cardiometabolic
problems to appear together. Its harmonised international definition is any three of the following
five, with no single obligatory component [@alberti2009harmonizingMetS]:

- central obesity: waist ≥90 cm (men) or ≥80 cm (women) in Asian populations;
- raised triglycerides: ≥1.7 mmol/L;
- low HDL cholesterol: <1.0 mmol/L (men) or <1.3 mmol/L (women);
- raised blood pressure: ≥130/85 mmHg;
- raised fasting glucose: ≥5.6 mmol/L.

Treatment for a component counts the same as an abnormal reading.

Two linked problems underlie the cluster: central fat and **insulin resistance**, a reduced response
of the body's cells to insulin. At first, the pancreas compensates by making more insulin to keep
blood glucose normal. These common underlying abnormalities are why the five components appear
together. The syndrome is therefore best regarded as a risk marker, not a single disease treated with a
single drug: it flags a markedly raised risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease
[@kaurMetsDefinitionsReview2014; @metsDefinitionsControversies2011]. The label is a prompt to look at
the whole cluster and its common underlying abnormalities. Local data add a further nuance: the
components do not always cluster in the same way across Singapore's ethnic groups
[@angMetsSingaporeNHS2005].

In the interactive below, toggle a patient's findings to see when the three-of-five threshold is met,
and how sleep loss and stress contribute to the same underlying abnormalities (drawn as the hub of the wheel).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does Singapore start intervening at a BMI of 23, when the WHO cut-offs call no one overweight until 25?
BMI cannot show how much of the weight is fat or where it sits. Singaporean adults carry more body
fat, and proportionally more visceral fat, at a given BMI than the Western populations behind the WHO
cut-offs. Asians therefore reach diabetes and cardiovascular risk at a lower BMI, so the WHO cut-offs
would miss real risk. The Yishun Study showed the gap: classifying by body fat flagged far more adults
than BMI did.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has raised blood pressure, low HDL and raised fasting glucose, but a waist under the cut-off. Does she have the metabolic syndrome, and what follows from the label?
Yes. The harmonised definition is any three of five components with no obligatory one, so central
obesity is not required. The label is a risk marker for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease,
so it prompts a look at the whole cluster and its common underlying abnormalities (insulin resistance
with central fat), not a single drug for "the syndrome".
:::

### How obesity produces the metabolic syndrome {#sec-mechanism}

The five problems occur together because body fat is an active endocrine organ: its location and
metabolic activity link central obesity to raised blood glucose. (The normal mechanics of fat storage and
insulin action are in the [*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd) and
[*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-switch) chapters; here we follow how they go
wrong.) Four terms describe the process:

Ectopic fat
: Fat deposited inside organs such as the liver and muscle, instead of under the skin.

Chronic low-grade inflammation
: A persistent, mild inflammatory state; in obesity it is driven by immune cells (macrophages)
  recruited into enlarged, stressed fat tissue.

Adipokines
: The hormones and signalling proteins that fat tissue releases. They include adiponectin, which is
  insulin-sensitising and anti-inflammatory.

Lipotoxicity
: The harm done when free fatty acids and ectopic lipid spill over into non-fat tissues; in liver and
  muscle it disrupts insulin signalling.

![How obesity produces the metabolic syndrome. A chronic energy surplus enlarges visceral and ectopic fat, which becomes inflamed and shifts its adipokine output, driving insulin resistance (the common underlying abnormality) and blunting satiety, so the five-component cluster emerges from one mechanism.](/figures/mechanisms/obesity-pathophysiology.svg){#fig-obesity-pathophysiology width="88%" fig-align="center"}

The chain starts with where the fat is stored. A chronic energy surplus enlarges fat cells, but the
harmful growth is in visceral fat, packed around the abdominal organs, and in ectopic fat, not in the
subcutaneous fat under the skin. Visceral fat drains straight to the liver and behaves differently
from subcutaneous fat: it is an independent marker of cardiometabolic risk, over and above BMI
[@neeland2019visceral]. Waist circumference, a simple bedside measure of central fat, therefore adds
information that BMI does not give.

Enlarged fat tissue then becomes inflamed. As fat cells enlarge and outgrow their blood supply, the
tissue becomes stressed and recruits macrophages, and develops chronic low-grade inflammation.
This adipose inflammation is now understood to cause insulin resistance rather than merely accompany
it [@hotamisligil2006inflammation]. The adipokine profile shifts at the same time: adiponectin falls,
while pro-inflammatory signals such as tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and
resistin rise [@ouchi2011adipokines].

The result is insulin resistance, the common underlying abnormality of the cluster. Alongside the
inflammation, lipotoxicity impairs insulin signalling in the liver and muscle
[@samuel2012mechanisms], and together they make the body's cells less responsive to insulin. Insulin
resistance raises blood glucose, drives the liver to over-produce triglyceride (raising triglycerides
and lowering HDL) and contributes to higher blood pressure, so the five components emerge from one
mechanism.

Fat also signals to the brain, and in obesity this signalling is impaired. Leptin, the satiety signal from
fat, is raised, but central leptin signalling is blunted. This leptin resistance (see the
[*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-leptin) chapter) weakens satiety
and makes the surplus harder to reverse [@myers2010leptin]. The same biology that produces the
cluster also makes the extra weight harder to lose, which is why lifestyle change is a physiological
intervention, not a test of willpower.

### Why weight accumulates: energy balance and diet quality {#sec-accumulation}

In thermodynamic terms, weight gain results from a chronic positive energy balance: small daily surpluses
accumulated over years (see the [*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd) chapter). "Eat less, move
more" is weak clinical advice on its own, however, because it addresses only the number of calories, not their source, and what
is eaten shapes how much gets eaten. Two dietary factors are the main contributors.

**Ultra-processed foods drive overeating even when the nutrients are matched.** The evidence comes
from the controlled inpatient trial met in the *Digestion and absorption* chapter. People freely eating
an ultra-processed diet took in about 500 kcal a day more than the same people on an unprocessed diet,
and gained weight, although the two diets were matched for sugar, fat, fibre and salt [@hall2019upf].
Higher ultra-processed intake is associated with obesity and, more convincingly, with incident diabetes and
cardiovascular outcomes across large populations [@lane2024upfumbrella].

**Energy from sugar-sweetened drinks is poorly compensated.** After a sugar-sweetened drink, people
do not eat correspondingly less at the next meal, and higher intake produces dose-dependent weight
gain [@nguyen2023ssb]. Swapping to a "diet" drink is not a reliable solution. The WHO advises
against relying on **non-sugar sweeteners**, the sugar substitutes in "diet" drinks, for weight
control, so the better swap is water or an unsweetened drink, plus habit change [@who2023nss].

The targets are simple to state: free sugars under 10% of energy (ideally under 5%), saturated fat
under 10%, *trans* fat under 1% and salt under 5 g a day [@who2020diet; @who2015sugars]. Singapore
translates them into tools that need no arithmetic: My Healthy Plate (a quarter wholegrains, a
quarter protein, half fruit and vegetables) and the Nutri-Grade A–D grades on drinks
[@hpbHealthyPlate; @hpbNutriGrade]. The emphasis is on dietary patterns rather than single nutrients, and on
minimally processed rather than ultra-processed food [@aha2021diet].

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: why "same nutrients" can still mean more energy eaten
Soft, energy-dense, quick-to-eat foods are eaten faster and in greater volume before fullness (satiety)
signals take effect, so intake can exceed need even when a diet is matched on sugar, fat and fibre.
In the inpatient feeding trial people ate the ultra-processed meals faster, a possible explanation
alongside the higher energy density of their solid foods; which feature matters most is still debated.
Either way, processing, as well as composition, is a modifiable factor in its own right [@hall2019upf].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
For many Singaporeans, most of these choices are made at the hawker centre. Many staples are energy-dense: a plate of char
kway teow provides roughly 744 kcal with about 38 g of fat, around two-thirds of a day's recommended fat (55–60 g) in one dish
[@healthhubHawkerSwaps]. Several lower-energy-density swaps still fit My Healthy Plate:

- thunder tea rice;
- non-fried yong tau foo (more vegetables and tofu, clear soup);
- sliced fish bee hoon soup;
- Teochew porridge with lean sides.

For drinks, read the Nutri-Grade: choose grade A or B, or order *kopi-o kosong*, *teh-o kosong* or
plain water instead of a grade C or D condensed-milk or bubble-tea drink.
:::

![Char kway teow, a Singapore hawker favourite and a useful energy-density reference point: roughly 744 kcal and 38 g of fat in one plate.](/figures/food/char-kway-teow.jpg){#fig-char-kway-teow width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two men have the same BMI, but one carries much more visceral fat. Why is he more likely to develop the metabolic-syndrome cluster?
Visceral fat drains straight to the liver and is an independent marker of cardiometabolic risk over
and above BMI. Enlarged visceral and ectopic fat becomes inflamed and shifts its adipokine output
(adiponectin falls, pro-inflammatory signals rise), and with lipotoxicity this produces insulin
resistance. Insulin resistance then raises glucose and triglycerides, lowers HDL and contributes to
higher blood pressure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: the inpatient trial matched its two diets for sugar, fat, fibre and salt. Why did people still eat about 500 kcal a day more on the ultra-processed diet, and what follows for advice?
Because the diets were matched on composition, the difference lies in the form of the food. Soft,
energy-dense, quick-to-eat foods are eaten faster and in greater volume before fullness (satiety)
signals take effect, though which of these features matters most is still debated. Processing, as
well as composition, is therefore a modifiable factor. Advice should target the overall dietary pattern:
minimally processed food over ultra-processed, and water or an unsweetened drink over a
sugar-sweetened one.
:::

## Dietary management: lifestyle intervention and weight-inclusive care {#sec-managing}

### Lifestyle intervention: the cornerstone of care {#sec-lifestyle}

The weight-loss target is modest. A sustained 5–10% weight loss yields a disproportionate,
dose-dependent cardiometabolic benefit, improving glucose, blood pressure and lipids well out of
proportion to the change on the scale [@wing2011modest]. Lifestyle change is the cornerstone of care:
every other treatment is added to it, not substituted for it.

Five areas of lifestyle change make up first-line care, and two of them, sleep and stress, are
routinely overlooked (see the
[*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-sleep-stress) chapter).

**Diet pattern.** The dietary change is a set of food substitutions based on My Healthy
Plate, not a branded diet, aiming for a 5–10% loss over 6–12 months [@aceBmiControl2026].

**Physical activity.** Activity has benefits partly independent of weight loss: it cuts visceral fat,
improves insulin sensitivity and preserves lean mass even when weight changes little
[@kolnes2021exercisefat]. Diet quality remains the larger influence on weight, so the two are paired.

**Sleep.** Sleep is a modifiable factor in weight. Short or poor sleep raises energy intake with no
matching rise in expenditure, and extending sleep brings intake back down [@alkhatib2017;
@tasali2022sleepextension]. Short habitual sleep is also associated with more central obesity
[@kohanmoo2024shortsleep]. The appetite-hormone mechanism is less certain: the classic account, in
which leptin falls and ghrelin rises, rests on a small early sleep-restriction experiment, but a 2025 meta-analysis of trials
found no reliable hormone shift [@spiegel2004; @sleepHormonesMeta2025]. The effect on intake
is consistent; the hormonal explanation is plausible but unproven.

**Stress.** Chronic stress and cortisol are thought to bias eating toward energy-dense comfort food
and promote abdominal fat deposition, a self-reinforcing cycle that would worsen central fat and insulin
resistance [@dallman2003]. The evidence is largely animal work and human associations, so the cycle
is plausible but not proven. Mindfulness programmes for weight are still exploratory, so the mechanism can be described
but an effective intervention cannot be promised [@daubenmier2011].

**Behaviour change.** Behaviour-change skills help patients sustain the other four changes (see the
[*Behaviour-change counselling*](behaviour-change-counselling.qmd) chapter).

Two cautions about the evidence apply to what lifestyle change can be expected to achieve. First, the landmark
trials showing that lifestyle change can prevent or even remit diabetes used intensive, structured
programmes. The Diabetes Prevention Program was a 16-session curriculum [@dpp2002], and DiRECT's ~46%
remission applied to early, non-insulin-treated patients and is untested in Asian primary care
[@lean2018direct]. Second, improving those risk factors is not the same as preventing cardiovascular
events: an intensive lifestyle programme in established diabetes improved markers but did not reduce
cardiovascular events [@lookahead2013]. (The mechanics of remission are in the *Type 2 diabetes*
chapter.)

### Weight-inclusive care: the framing is part of the treatment {#sec-weight-inclusive}

How a weight conversation is framed changes its outcome, so framing is a clinical skill.
**Weight stigma** is negative attitudes towards, and treatment of, people because of their weight,
such as blame, shaming or disrespect. Weight stigma is a health hazard [@tomiyama2014cobwebs;
@phelan2015impact; @puhl2023barriers]:

- it degrades the quality of care;
- it drives patients to avoid appointments;
- by raising cortisol and comfort-eating, it is thought to promote weight gain paradoxically, the cycle proposed
  by the Cyclic Obesity/Weight-Based Stigma (COBWEBS) model.

An international consensus of experts now condemns weight stigma outright and asks clinicians to switch focus from
the scale to health and behaviour [@rubino2020consensus; @tylka2014weightinclusive;
@batterham2020switchingfocus]. Care built on that shift is **weight-inclusive**: it bases counselling on
health behaviours and metabolic markers instead of on the scale alone. Weight stigma is also common
in Singapore: in a local survey most respondents had felt weight-stigmatised, and a fifth felt
disrespected or discouraged by a healthcare worker [@chue2022stigmasg; @goff2023sgweightbias].

::: {.callout-important}
## Person-first, permission-based framing
The framing comes down to three habits [@weghuber2023peoplefirst; @batterham2020switchingfocus]:

- Use **person-first language**, which names the person before the condition ("a person with
  obesity", not "an obese patient").
- Ask permission before discussing weight.
- Set goals around health behaviours and metabolic markers, not the scale alone, while still keeping
  the ~5–10% target that brings the metabolic benefit.

Shaming does not motivate weight loss and may promote weight gain.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has lost 6% of his weight, but his BMI still puts him in the high-risk band. Why is the loss still worthwhile?
A sustained 5–10% loss gives a disproportionate, dose-dependent cardiometabolic benefit, improving
glucose, blood pressure and lipids well out of proportion to the change on the scale. Physical
activity adds to this, cutting visceral fat and improving insulin sensitivity even when weight changes
little. The target is metabolic health.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can shaming a patient about weight make the weight harder to lose?
Weight stigma degrades the quality of care and drives patients to avoid appointments, so they receive
less of the care that helps. Stigma is also thought to raise cortisol and comfort-eating, which can
promote weight gain (the cycle proposed by the COBWEBS model). Person-first, permission-based framing is therefore
part of the treatment.
:::

## When to refer {#sec-obesity-refer}

Lifestyle change remains the basis of care at every step; the specialist tiers above it are reached by
referral.

::: {.callout-note}
## Stepped care: medication, surgery and referral
Above lifestyle change are two specialist tiers: anti-obesity medication (including the newer GLP-1
receptor agonists) and **metabolic-bariatric surgery** (weight-loss surgery), which can achieve
substantially greater loss for selected patients [@lee2023obesitylandscape]. The task at this stage
is to **recognise that these tiers exist and refer**, not to prescribe or select them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with obesity asks you to start her on a GLP-1 drug. What is your role at this stage?
Anti-obesity medication, including the GLP-1 receptor agonists, and metabolic-bariatric surgery are
specialist tiers that sit above lifestyle change. The task at this stage is to recognise that these
tiers exist and refer, not to prescribe or select them. Lifestyle change stays the cornerstone: the
other treatments are added to it, not substituted for it.
:::

## Is obesity just "eating too much"? {#sec-close}

The belief comes from the principle of energy balance: weight is gained only when intake exceeds
expenditure, so obesity looks like a matter of eating less. The principle is correct, but it leaves out
three things. What is eaten shapes how much is eaten, because ultra-processed foods and
sugar-sweetened drinks increase intake beyond need. Once the surplus is stored, leptin resistance weakens
satiety and makes the higher weight harder to lose. And the harm depends on where the fat is stored: visceral
and ectopic fat drive the insulin resistance behind the metabolic-syndrome cluster. Singaporean
adults carry more visceral fat at a given BMI, which is why Singapore interprets BMI at lower cut-offs and
always alongside waist circumference.

Care therefore addresses those causes, and the way it is delivered matters too: because weight stigma
can itself promote weight gain, weight-inclusive, person-first care is part of the treatment.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**Singapore reports obesity at one threshold and acts at another.** Population obesity is reported at
the WHO ≥30 threshold for international comparability, and on that measure it rose from 10.5% to
12.7% between 2019–20 and 2023–24; clinical action starts at a much lower BMI, and the ≥27.5 high-risk band
has stayed broadly stable at just over 1 in 5 adults (20.7% to 22.8%) [@mohNPHS2024]. The 12.7% figure is used for international comparison; the
≥27.5 and ≥23 cut-offs are the ones used in clinical practice. Over the same period, national physical activity recovered to 84.7%
and obesity still rose, local evidence for putting diet quality ahead of "just
exercise more" [@mohNPHS2024].

**The components of the cluster are common.** The survey reports the components separately.
Hypertension affects about 1 in 3 adults, raised blood lipids about 1 in 3 and
diabetes roughly 1 in 11: the population figures behind the clustering of these risk factors [@mohNPHS2024].

**Obesity and diabetes follow an ethnic gradient.** Malay and Indian residents have markedly higher rates of
obesity and diabetes than Chinese residents [@zhang2024bmiSg]. The contributing factors are
genetic, socio-economic, dietary and environmental, not moral, and the gradient motivates culturally tailored
counselling and the national War on Diabetes [@mohWarOnDiabetes]. (The diabetes detail is in the
*Type 2 diabetes* chapter.)

**National policy gives clinicians tools to point patients toward.** The tools include My Healthy
Plate, Nutri-Grade (whose national roll-out measurably cut the sugar in drinks bought)
[@moh2023nutrigradeimpact; @shin2023nutrigrade] and the Healthier Choice Symbol on packaged foods
[@hpbHealthierChoiceSymbol]. Healthier SG, the enrolled-family-doctor scheme, builds "recognise and
refer" into a longitudinal health plan [@mohHealthierSG].

The 2016 obesity guideline's Asian BMI cut-offs remain current, but its treatment sections predate
the GLP-1 era, so its management content is dated [@hpbmoh2016obesityCPG; @lee2023obesitylandscape].
